summary: Specifies NETBLT (NETwork BLock Transfer), a transport-level protocol for quickly moving large amounts of data between computers. It is reliable, flow controlled and aims for high throughput over many kinds of networks. It was experimental, not a standard, and some parts were unfinished. It revises RFC 969.

plainLanguage.summary: NETBLT is a proposed way to transfer large amounts of data reliably using groups of packets called buffers. It paces packet bursts and lets the receiver request only packets that are missing.

subtitle: A bulk-transfer design that sends large buffers in paced packets and requests only missing data again.

tldr.problem: Large transfers over long-delay or lossy networks can waste time if they depend on small windows or retransmit too much data.
tldr.mechanism: NETBLT divides a transfer into buffers and packets, paces packet bursts at a negotiated rate, and lets the receiver list missing packets for retransmission.
tldr.outcome: RFC 998 is an Experimental revision of RFC 969, published for discussion. It says some parts were unspecified and advises against implementation.

today: RFC 998 is an Experimental revision of RFC 969, published for discussion and comment rather than as a standard. Its Status section says parts were not specified and implementation was not advised.

sections.title: What NETBLT Is For
sections.content:
NETBLT (NETwork BLock Transfer) is a transport-level protocol intended to transfer large amounts of data between computers. It aims to provide reliable, flow-controlled transfer over different networks, including paths with long delays or packet loss.

The protocol opens a connection, transfers data in large aggregates called buffers and then closes the connection. The client supplies data a buffer at a time, so interaction with NETBLT occurs per buffer rather than per packet. The RFC says the maximum transfer length is 2**32 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: NETBLT sends a large transfer as a sequence of buffers, each made up of packets. The design aims to keep data moving while detecting and repairing missing packets.

sections.title: Buffers, Packets and the Last Packet
sections.content:
The sender and receiver negotiate a buffer size during connection setup. Each buffer is split into DATA packets of a negotiated size, except that the final packet in each buffer uses the LDATA type. DATA and LDATA have the same structure apart from their type, and LDATA lets the receiver identify the buffer's end.

NETBLT does not keep a copy of a buffer for retransmission; it copies requested data again from the client's buffer. Packets should be large enough for efficient transfer but not so large that they cause internetwork fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: A buffer is divided into packets, and its final packet is marked LDATA. If packets are missing, NETBLT can copy those portions again from the client's buffer.

sections.title: Rate Control and Multiple Buffers
sections.content:
NETBLT controls the sending rate in bursts rather than allowing a fixed window of packets. The sender transmits a negotiated burst size over a negotiated burst interval, using timers instead of receiver messages to pace the packets. Packet size, buffer size, burst size and burst rate are negotiated during setup; the passive end may make proposed values more restrictive.

With one buffer at a time, the sender waits for confirmation before starting the next buffer. Multiple buffering allows it to begin later buffers while earlier ones await confirmation or retransmission requests. The RFC says burst sizes of five to ten packets should keep overhead acceptable on many modern operating systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends agree how many packets to send in each burst and how often to send a burst. Multiple buffers let the sender continue while an earlier buffer awaits confirmation.

sections.title: Opening, Transferring and Closing
sections.content:
The active end opens a connection with an OPEN packet. The passive end replies with RESPONSE or REFUSED. During setup, the ends negotiate transfer parameters, maximum concurrent buffers, data-checksum behavior and death-timeout values. The OPEN includes a 32-bit connection identifier that must be returned in RESPONSE.

For each buffer, the receiver sends GO when ready. The sender transmits DATA and LDATA packets; the receiver returns RESEND with missing packets or OK when the buffer is complete. A successful transfer marks the last buffer, waits for confirmations and then closes; clients can also send QUIT, and a malfunctioning NETBLT layer can send ABORT.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints first agree on transfer settings. The receiver signals when a buffer is ready, and later confirms it or lists packets that need to be sent again.

sections.title: Timers and Loss Recovery
sections.content:
Control messages such as GO, OK and RESEND travel in CONTROL packets with sequence numbers. A control timer lets the receiver resend an unacknowledged control packet. The sender returns the highest consecutive control-message sequence number it has received.

The receiver also runs a data timer for each buffer. If it expires before the buffer is complete, the receiver sends RESEND for missing packets. A death timer is reset whenever a packet arrives; when a NETBLT has nothing else to send, it uses KEEPALIVE packets so the other end does not assume it has failed.
sections.plainLanguage: Timers let the receiver repeat lost control messages and ask for missing data. KEEPALIVE packets show that an otherwise quiet endpoint is still active.
